title: The Fatimid Caliphate
subtitle: 909–1171 · The Ismaili Counter-Caliphate, Cairo and the Red Sea World

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: An Ismaili line of caliph-imams — and, from the great crisis of the 1070s, the viziers who ran the state

entries.label: Al-Mahdi founds the dynasty in Ifriqiya
entries.hint: The Ismaili missionary movement, organised for decades in secret, brought its hidden imam out of hiding in 909: backed by the Kutama Berbers, Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i overthrew the Aghlabids and installed Abd Allah as al-Mahdi, caliph and imam. A third man now claimed to be the sole rightful leader of all Muslims.
entries.note: The founding narrative survives mainly in later Ismaili works — the 'Iftitah al-Da'wa' of al-Qadi al-Nu'man (d. 974, close to events) and the 'Sira' of the chamberlain Ja'far — and in the hostile Sunni tradition. Halm, 'The Empire of the Mahdi: The Rise of the Fatimids' (1996), is the standard reconstruction.

entries.label: Al-Qa'im, al-Mansur and the revolt of Abu Yazid
entries.hint: A Kharijite Berber rising under Abu Yazid, 'the man on the donkey', overran Ifriqiya and besieged the Fatimids in Mahdia for months in 944–45 — the dynasty's closest brush with extinction. Al-Mansur broke the revolt, founded a new capital, al-Mansuriyya, and stabilised the state for the conquest of Egypt.
entries.note: al-Nu'man; the Sunni sources are sympathetic to Abu Yazid as a scourge of heretics. Halm (1996).

entries.label: Al-Mu'izz conquers Egypt and builds Cairo
entries.hint: Al-Mu'izz's general Jawhar took Egypt from the failing Ikhshidids in 969 without a battle worth the name, laid out a new walled palace-city, al-Qahira ('the Victorious'), and founded al-Azhar as its congregational mosque. The caliph followed in 973, and the Fatimid centre of gravity moved east for good.
entries.note: al-Nu'man; Ibn al-Athir; the founding of al-Azhar and Cairo (Rabbat; Sanders, 'Ritual, Politics, and the City in Fatimid Cairo', 1994). The main narrative source, al-Maqrizi's 'Itti'az al-Hunafa', is 15th-century.

entries.label: Al-Aziz — the empire at its widest
entries.hint: Under al-Aziz the Fatimid name was read in the Friday prayer from Ifriqiya to Damascus, Mecca and Medina and, briefly, Mosul. He staffed the state with Christians and Jews — his vizier Ya'qub ibn Killis was a convert from Judaism — and married a Christian whose brothers he made patriarchs of Jerusalem and Alexandria.
entries.note: al-Musabbihi (d. 1030), the great contemporary Cairo chronicler, is mostly lost; what survives is quoted by al-Maqrizi and Ibn Muyassar. Lev, 'State and Society in Fatimid Egypt' (1991).

entries.label: Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah
entries.hint: Al-Hakim ruled by sudden, contradictory decree: persecutions of Sunnis, then of Christians and Jews (he had the Church of the Holy Sepulchre destroyed in 1009), then reversals and restitution; bans on chess, on certain foods, on women leaving their houses. In 1021 he rode into the Muqattam hills at night and never returned. A movement that held him divine became the Druze.
entries.note: al-Musabbihi (fragmentary) is the contemporary witness; the fuller accounts are later and hostile or apologetic. Walker, 'Caliph of Cairo: al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah' (2009), is the careful modern study.

entries.label: Al-Zahir, Sitt al-Mulk and the drift
entries.hint: Al-Hakim's formidable sister Sitt al-Mulk governed as regent for the boy al-Zahir and steadied the state after the chaos of the previous reign. Her death in 1023 left the government to a rotating set of officials and the beginnings of the long weakening that the next reign would nearly complete.
entries.note: Cortese & Calderini, 'Women and the Fatimids in the World of Islam' (2006), on Sitt al-Mulk; the sources are thin and mostly later.

entries.label: Al-Mustansir — the 58-year reign and the collapse
entries.hint: The longest reign in Islamic history spanned the dynasty's ruin and rescue: seven years of Nile failure and famine in the 1060s, the army's Turkish, Berber and Sudanese regiments fighting each other through a starving Cairo, the loss of Ifriqiya and then Syria — until the Armenian general Badr al-Jamali seized the state in 1074 and held it together by force.
entries.note: Nasir Khusraw's 'Safarnama' describes Cairo at its height in 1047 — a rare contemporary eyewitness; the crisis is in al-Maqrizi and Ibn Muyassar, drawing on lost contemporary work. Brett, 'The Fatimid Empire' (2017).

entries.label: The Nizari–Musta'li split and al-Musta'li
entries.hint: When al-Mustansir died, the vizier al-Afdal set aside the designated heir Nizar and enthroned his younger, more pliable brother al-Musta'li. Nizar revolted from Alexandria, was defeated and walled up alive. The Ismaili world split permanently: the Fatimids continued as Musta'li imams, while the Persian and Syrian da'wa — and the Assassins — followed the line of Nizar.
entries.note: the pro-Nizari and pro-Musta'li traditions are irreconcilable. Daftary, 'The Ismailis: Their History and Doctrines' (2nd ed. 2007), chs. 5–6. Cross-references the Nizari entries in the Abbasid folio.

entries.label: Al-Amir to al-Adid — the caliphate as a token
entries.hint: The last five caliphs were installed as children and kept as sacred figureheads while viziers fought for the palace. Al-Amir was murdered by Nizari agents in 1130, splitting the Musta'li da'wa again (Hafizi vs Tayyibi). By the 1160s the caliph was a prize contested between Crusader Jerusalem and Zangid Syria.
entries.note: Ibn Muyassar and al-Maqrizi; Ibn al-Qalanisi of Damascus is contemporary for the 12th century. The Hafizi/Tayyibi split: Daftary (2007).

entries.label: Ya'qub ibn Killis builds the Fatimid state
entries.hint: A convert to Islam from a Baghdadi Jewish family, Ibn Killis organised Fatimid Egypt's finances, its land tax, its chancery and its court ceremonial, and turned al-Azhar into a teaching institution with salaried scholars. He is the architect of the administration the dynasty ran on for two centuries.
entries.note: al-Musabbihi (via al-Maqrizi); the 'Sira' of Ibn Killis partly survives. Lev, 'State and Society in Fatimid Egypt' (1991).

entries.label: Badr al-Jamali — the vizier of the sword
entries.hint: Summoned from Acre with his Armenian troops, Badr al-Jamali crushed the mutinous regiments, ended the famine-era anarchy, rebuilt Cairo's stone walls and gates, and made the vizierate a military dictatorship — 'amir of the armies, director of the missionaries, guide of the judges'. The caliph kept the sanctity; the vizier kept the power.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi; the surviving Cairo gates (Bab al-Futuh, Bab al-Nasr, Bab Zuwayla, 1087) carry his building inscriptions — contemporary documentary evidence. Brett (2017).

entries.label: Al-Afdal Shahanshah
entries.hint: Badr's son ruled Egypt for twenty-seven years. He engineered the 1094 succession that split the Ismailis, retook Jerusalem from the Seljuks in 1098 — a year before the Crusaders took it from him — and fought the Franks for the Palestinian coast until he was assassinated in a Cairo street in 1121.
entries.note: Ibn al-Qalanisi; Ibn Muyassar. Whether the caliph al-Amir or the Nizaris ordered his killing is disputed in the sources.

entries.label: The vizier-warlords
entries.hint: After al-Afdal the vizierate was seized by force again and again — al-Ma'mun al-Bata'ihi, Ridwan, Ibn Sallar, the regicide Abbas, and Tala'i ibn Ruzzik, a general who was also a respected poet. Each ruled as regent for a boy caliph; most died violently. The state consumed its own leadership.
entries.note: Ibn Muyassar; al-Maqrizi. Tala'i ibn Ruzzik's poetry survives (Diwan, ed. Muhammad Hadi al-Amini).

entries.label: Shawar, Dirgham and the invitation of foreign armies
entries.hint: The last vizier war — Shawar against Dirgham — dragged in both Amalric of Jerusalem and Nur al-Din of Aleppo. Over three campaigns (1164–1169) Zangid and Crusader armies marched up and down Egypt; Fustat was burned by its own governor to deny it to the Franks (1168); and the Zangid general Shirkuh emerged as vizier.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir (Zangid-sympathetic); William of Tyre for the Crusader side; Abu Shama's compilation.

entries.label: Saladin ends the caliphate
entries.hint: Shirkuh died within months; his nephew Saladin became vizier for the fourteen-year-old al-Adid. In September 1171 Saladin had the Friday sermon read in the name of the Abbasid caliph; al-Adid died days later, probably not knowing. Egypt was Sunni again, and the Ismaili caliphate — 262 years old — was over.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; Ibn Abi Tayy (a Shia of Aleppo, a rare sympathetic voice, surviving in quotation). Lyons & Jackson, 'Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War' (1982). Cross-references the Ayyubid and Mamluk material in the Abbasid folio.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Abu Yazid, the conquest of Egypt, the Qarmatian invasions, al-Hakim's Jerusalem, and the wars for Palestine

entries.label: The revolt of Abu Yazid
entries.hint: A Zanata Berber schoolmaster preaching a rigorist Kharijite Islam raised the tribes of the Aurès against the Fatimids, took Kairouan, and besieged the caliph al-Qa'im in Mahdia. Al-Mansur's counter-offensive, and Abu Yazid's death in the mountains in 947, saved a dynasty that had come within a wall of ending.
entries.note: al-Qadi al-Nu'man's account, written for the victors; the Sunni sources present Abu Yazid as an orthodox hero. Halm, 'The Empire of the Mahdi' (1996).

entries.label: Jawhar takes Egypt
entries.hint: With the Ikhshidid state broken by famine and succession failure, the Fatimid general Jawhar al-Siqilli marched from Ifriqiya, negotiated the surrender of Fustat, and began laying out the palace-city and al-Azhar the same year. It was the least costly conquest of a great province in the medieval Islamic world.
entries.note: al-Nu'man; the 'aman' (safe-conduct) Jawhar granted Fustat is preserved in the sources and is a Fatimid governing document. Brett, 'The Rise of the Fatimids' (2001).

entries.label: The Qarmatians invade Egypt
entries.hint: The Qarmatians of eastern Arabia, though fellow Ismailis, rejected the Fatimid claim to the imamate and twice invaded Egypt, reaching the walls of the new capital. Jawhar's defence in 971 and al-Mu'izz's victory in 974 secured the Fatimid hold — and turned two branches of one movement into enemies.
entries.note: al-Nu'man; the Fatimid–Qarmatian rupture is central to Madelung, 'The Fatimids and the Qarmatis of Bahrayn' (1996). Cross-references the Qarmatian entries in the Islamic Eastern Arabia folio.

entries.label: The long contest for Aleppo and Damascus
entries.hint: Fatimid Syria was never secure: the Hamdanids of Aleppo, Bedouin confederations, Byzantine emperors campaigning south, and the Fatimids' own Turkish and Berber troops all fought over it for decades. Aleppo became a Byzantine protectorate; Damascus revolted repeatedly. The northern frontier drained the treasury without ever being fixed.
entries.note: Yahya of Antioch (an Egyptian Christian who moved to Byzantine Antioch — a contemporary writing across the confessional and political divide) is the essential source. Bianquis, 'Damas et la Syrie sous la domination fatimide' (1986–89).

entries.label: The destruction of the Holy Sepulchre
entries.hint: Al-Hakim ordered the Church of the Holy Sepulchre razed to the rock. Later restored under his successor with Byzantine money and permission, the act nonetheless entered Latin memory as an outrage against Christendom and is counted among the long-fuse causes of the First Crusade eighty years later.
entries.note: Yahya of Antioch (contemporary, detailed); the Latin chroniclers writing after 1095 magnified it. Canard, 'La destruction de l'église de la Résurrection', Byzantion (1965); Walker, 'Caliph of Cairo' (2009).

entries.label: The army's civil wars and the starving of Cairo
entries.hint: Seven years of low Nile met a fractured army — Turkish, Berber and Black African regiments that had stopped obeying anyone. They fought each other through the capital, looted the palace treasuries, and blockaded the food supply. Contemporaries describe famine, plague and, in the worst reports, cannibalism. The Fatimid state effectively dissolved until Badr al-Jamali reconstituted it by force.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi's 'Itti'az' and 'Khitat', drawing on lost contemporary chronicles; the crisis ('al-shidda al-mustansiriyya') is a set-piece of the later tradition and its darkest details should be read with that in mind. Brett (2017).

entries.label: The Seljuks take Fatimid Syria and Palestine
entries.hint: As the Fatimid state collapsed inward, the Seljuk Turks and their allied emirs took Damascus (1076), Jerusalem and most of Palestine. Al-Afdal recovered Jerusalem and Ascalon from them only in 1098 — just in time to lose Jerusalem to the Crusaders the following year.
entries.note: Ibn al-Qalanisi (contemporary Damascus); Ibn al-Athir. The Seljuk–Fatimid frontier war is the backdrop to the Crusade's success (Hillenbrand, 'The Crusades: Islamic Perspectives', 1999).

entries.label: The Crusaders take Jerusalem; the Battle of Ascalon
entries.hint: The First Crusade stormed Fatimid Jerusalem in July 1099 and massacred its population. Al-Afdal's relief army arrived weeks late and was routed outside Ascalon in August. The Fatimids had misjudged the Franks as a possible counterweight to the Seljuks, and lost the holy city they had held for a year.
entries.note: Ibn al-Qalanisi; the Latin 'Gesta Francorum'; al-Azimi. The Fatimid earlier contacts with the Crusaders (the 1098 embassy) are noted in both traditions.

entries.label: The fifty-year war for the coast
entries.loc: the Palestinian and Egyptian coast; the Nile mouths
entries.hint: The Fatimids held the coastal cities one by one until they could not: Acre fell in 1104, Sidon in 1110, Tyre in 1124, and finally Ascalon — the forward base for raiding into the crusader kingdom, resupplied by fleet four times a year — in 1153. The Fatimid navy fought on but the strategic initiative was gone.
entries.note: Ibn al-Qalanisi; William of Tyre. The Fatimid navy and the Ascalon supply system (Lev, 'The Fatimid Navy', 1984).

entries.label: The Zangid–Crusader contest for Egypt
entries.hint: Three times between 1164 and 1169 the Zangid general Shirkuh and King Amalric of Jerusalem marched armies into Egypt, each invited by one Fatimid faction against the other. The last campaign ended with Fustat burned by its own governor, Amalric bought off, and Shirkuh — then Saladin — installed as the caliph's vizier.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; William of Tyre, who was close to the Jerusalem court's Egyptian policy. Lyons & Jackson, 'Saladin' (1982), chs. 1–2.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The da'wa hierarchy, a written Ismaili law, the iqta and the ceremonial state

entries.label: Al-Nu'man codifies Ismaili law
entries.hint: The chief judge al-Qadi al-Nu'man compiled the 'Pillars of Islam' (Da'a'im al-Islam), the official law code of the Fatimid state — a full Shia jurisprudence with the living imam as its ultimate authority. It is still the law of the Bohra and other Musta'li Ismaili communities today.
entries.note: al-Nu'man, 'Da'a'im al-Islam' (trans. Fyzee & Poonawala, 'The Pillars of Islam', 2002–04). Poonawala, 'al-Qadi al-Nu'man and Isma'ili Jurisprudence', in Daftary (ed.), 'Mediaeval Isma'ili History and Thought' (1996).

entries.label: The da'wa — a hierarchy of missionaries
entries.loc: from Cairo across the Islamic world
entries.hint: The Fatimid state ran a graded missionary organisation — a chief da'i in Cairo directing regional da'is who directed local ones, each initiate bound by an oath and led up through 'sessions of wisdom' at the palace. It reached from the Maghreb to Sind, working openly where the Fatimids ruled and in deep secret in Abbasid lands.
entries.note: the da'wa manuals — al-Nu'man's 'Kitab al-Himma', the 'Majalis' of al-Mu'ayyad al-Shirazi; Halm, 'The Fatimids and their Traditions of Learning' (1997).

entries.label: The gold dinar as international money
entries.hint: The Fatimid dinar, struck from West African gold and held to a strict standard, became the most trusted coin in the medieval Mediterranean — the 'bezant' that Italian and Byzantine merchants preferred and that Crusader states later imitated. Sound money was an instrument of Fatimid reach.
entries.note: the Fatimid gold coinage (Nicol, 'A Corpus of Fatimid Coins', 2006); the imitation dinars of Genoa, the Crusader states and Norman Sicily. The Geniza documents price everything in Fatimid dinars.

entries.label: Badr al-Jamali and the iqta
entries.hint: To pay an army the bankrupt treasury could not fund in cash, Badr al-Jamali assigned officers the tax revenue of districts directly (iqta) and had the whole of Egypt re-surveyed. It militarised the countryside and set the fiscal pattern the Ayyubids and Mamluks would inherit.
entries.note: the survey ('rawk') tradition; Rabie, 'The Financial System of Egypt AH 564–741' (1972), for the later development; Sato, 'State and Rural Society in Medieval Islam' (1997).

entries.label: The dhimma under the Fatimids — and under al-Hakim
entries.hint: For most of the dynasty, Christians and Jews served at the highest levels — as viziers, physicians, financiers and secretaries — and the Coptic and Jewish communities flourished. Al-Hakim's decade of persecution (forced conversions, the yellow badge, the church demolitions) was a violent exception that his own successors reversed.
entries.note: the contrast is documented in the Geniza (for the Jewish side) and in Coptic sources (the 'History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria'); Yahya of Antioch on al-Hakim. Rustow, 'The Lost Archive: Traces of a Caliphate in a Cairo Synagogue' (2020).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The imam as the living truth, the philosopher-missionaries, the Druze, and a Sunni majority left alone

entries.label: The imam as the living interpreter
entries.hint: Ismaili doctrine held that scripture and law (the zahir) are the outer shell of a hidden truth (the batin) that only the imam of the age — present, infallible, descended from Ali and Fatima — can unlock. The Fatimid caliph was not merely a ruler with religious authority; he was, to his followers, the axis on which the cosmos turned.
entries.note: the doctrine as set out in al-Nu'man's 'Ta'wil al-Da'a'im' and the da'wa literature; Daftary, 'The Ismailis' (2007), chs. 4–5; Halm, 'Shi'ism' (2nd ed. 2004).

entries.label: Al-Qadi al-Nu'man and the founding texts
entries.hint: Al-Nu'man served four caliphs as judge and propagandist and wrote the corpus the Fatimid religious state stood on: the law code, its allegorical interpretation, the history of the da'wa, the etiquette of the missionary, and the record of the imams' teaching sessions.
entries.note: al-Nu'man, 'Da'a'im al-Islam', 'Ta'wil al-Da'a'im', 'Iftitah al-Da'wa', 'Kitab al-Majalis wa'l-Musayarat'; Poonawala's bio-bibliography in Daftary (ed.) (1996).

entries.label: The philosopher-missionaries
entries.hint: Ismaili thinkers wove Neoplatonism into the doctrine of the imamate: Abu Ya'qub al-Sijistani's cosmology of the Word, and above all Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani's 'Repose of the Intellect' (c.1020), which mapped the ten cosmic intellects onto the ten highest ranks of the da'wa. Kirmani also wrote against the Cairo extremists who were beginning to call al-Hakim God.
entries.note: al-Kirmani, 'Rahat al-Aql'; Walker, 'Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani' (1999) and 'Early Philosophical Shiism' (1993, on al-Sijistani).
keywords: Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani Repose of the Intellect

entries.label: The Druze — the movement around al-Hakim
entries.loc: Cairo; then Mount Lebanon and the Hawran
entries.hint: A group of da'is — Hamza ibn Ali, and the man the movement is named after, al-Darazi — began preaching around 1017 that al-Hakim was the incarnation of the divine. Suppressed in Egypt after al-Hakim's disappearance, the movement 'closed its door' to new members in 1043 and survived as a secretive community in the mountains of Syria and Lebanon.
entries.note: the Druze scriptures ('Rasa'il al-Hikma') are the internal source; Firro, 'A History of the Druzes' (1992); Halm on the movement's Fatimid origins.

entries.label: The da'wa splits — Nizari, Hafizi, Tayyibi
entries.hint: Two succession disputes fractured the movement: 1094 sent the Persian and Syrian da'wa off after Nizar (the future Assassins), and 1130 split the remaining Musta'lis into a Hafizi branch loyal to the Cairo caliphs and a Tayyibi branch that held the true imam was in hiding and entrusted its leadership to the Sulayhid queen of Yemen.
entries.note: Daftary, 'The Ismailis' (2007), chs. 5–6; the Tayyibi transfer to Yemen and later India (the Bohras).

entries.label: The Sunni majority the Fatimids did not convert
entries.hint: Al-Azhar taught Ismaili law, but most Egyptians stayed Sunni — mainly Maliki, with a growing Shafi'i minority — and the Fatimid state, unlike a modern one, made little effort to change that. Two centuries of Ismaili rule left Egypt's population Sunni, which is why Saladin's restoration in 1171 met almost no resistance.
entries.note: Lev, 'State and Society in Fatimid Egypt' (1991); Brett, 'The Fatimid Empire' (2017), on the limits of the da'wa within Egypt itself.

entries.label: The Coptic church under Fatimid rule
entries.loc: Cairo; the monasteries of Wadi Natrun and Upper Egypt
entries.hint: The Coptic Orthodox church, still the faith of much of the Egyptian countryside, kept its patriarch (who moved his seat to Cairo), its monasteries and its scribes, and supplied the Fatimid administration with clerks and financiers. Al-Hakim's persecution aside, the Fatimid centuries were a period of Coptic cultural consolidation, including the shift of the liturgy toward Arabic.
entries.note: the 'History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria' (a continuously updated Coptic chronicle, contemporary from this period); den Heijer's studies; Swanson, 'The Coptic Papacy in Islamic Egypt' (2010).

entries.label: The Jewish communities and the Palestinian and Babylonian rites
entries.hint: Fatimid Egypt was the centre of Mediterranean Jewish life. The head of the Jews (ra'is al-yahud), often a court physician, was recognised by the caliph; the Palestinian and Babylonian rabbinic academies both operated; and the Karaite minority was wealthy and prominent. The Ben Ezra synagogue's storeroom preserved the papers of that world — the Cairo Geniza.
entries.note: Goitein, 'A Mediterranean Society' (1967–93); Rustow, 'Heresy and the Politics of Community: The Jews of the Fatimid Caliphate' (2008) and 'The Lost Archive' (2020).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Cairo the palace-city, al-Azhar and al-Aqmar, rock crystal, and the ceremonial calendar

entries.label: Cairo — the walled palace-city
entries.hint: Cairo began as a rectangle of mud-brick wall enclosing two vast palaces, a parade ground, the caliph's household and the elite regiments — a royal city closed to the ordinary population of Fustat next door. Badr al-Jamali rebuilt the walls and three monumental gates in dressed stone in 1087, in a style his Armenian engineers brought from the Byzantine frontier.
entries.note: the surviving northern gates (Bab al-Futuh, Bab al-Nasr) and Bab Zuwayla; Creswell, 'The Muslim Architecture of Egypt' vol. 1 (1952); Sanders, 'Ritual, Politics, and the City in Fatimid Cairo' (1994).

entries.label: Al-Azhar and the Fatimid mosque
entries.hint: Al-Azhar was the congregational mosque of the new capital and a school of the da'wa; the al-Hakim mosque gave the city a second great sanctuary; and the small al-Aqmar mosque of 1125 has the first fully composed decorative street facade in Cairo — the mosque stepping out to address the passer-by.
entries.note: al-Azhar's Fatimid core survives behind later additions; al-Aqmar's facade (Williams, 'The Cult of Alid Saints in the Fatimid Monuments of Cairo', 1985).

entries.label: Fatimid rock crystal
entries.hint: Fatimid lapidaries carved ewers, bottles and lamps from single flawless blocks of quartz, worked so thin the light passed through — the finest rock crystal ever made anywhere. When the palace treasuries were looted in the 1060s crisis, these objects scattered across the Mediterranean and ended up in the church treasuries of Venice, Aachen and Limburg.
entries.note: the seven signed Fatimid crystal ewers (Venice, Florence, the V&A, the Louvre); Contadini, 'Fatimid Art at the Victoria and Albert Museum' (1998); Hahn on the church-treasury afterlives.

entries.label: Lustre pottery, carved wood and tiraz
entries.hint: Fustat's workshops produced lustre-painted bowls with courtly and figural scenes, carved wooden panels and beams (some with painted hunting scenes from the palace), and inscribed tiraz textiles issued as robes of honour. Fatimid ornament — a lively, peopled style — spread to Norman Sicily and beyond.
entries.note: the Fustat ceramic finds (Bahgat & Massoul); the Cairo woodwork (the mihrab of Sayyida Ruqayya); Bloom, 'Arts of the City Victorious' (2007).

entries.label: The Fatimid ceremonial calendar
entries.loc: Cairo; the Nilometer at Rawda; the canal
entries.hint: The Fatimid state governed by procession: the caliph rode out under parasols and drums for the two Eids, the opening of the Nile canal, the Nilometer readings, Ashura and — a festival the Fatimids may have originated — the mawlid, the Prophet's birthday. The city's year was a liturgy performed by the imam.
entries.note: Ibn al-Tuwayr's 'Nuzhat al-Muqlatayn' (a late-Fatimid chancery official — near-primary for the ceremonial); al-Maqrizi's 'Khitat'; Sanders (1994).

entries.label: The poets of the da'wa and the court
entries.hint: Ibn Hani al-Andalusi, hailed as the Fatimid answer to al-Mutanabbi, praised al-Mu'izz in verse that verged on deifying him; the Persian traveller-poet Nasir Khusraw became a da'i and wrote philosophical odes; and the vizier Tala'i ibn Ruzzik was a respected poet in his own right. Ismaili doctrine gave Fatimid panegyric a cosmic register unlike anywhere else.
entries.note: Ibn Hani, Diwan; Nasir Khusraw, 'Diwan' and 'Safarnama'; the Fatimid poetic tradition (Sperl & Shackle, 'Qasida Poetry in Islamic Asia and Africa', 1996).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Ibn al-Haytham and the science of light, the Hakimi star tables, and the House of Knowledge

entries.label: Ibn al-Haytham and the Book of Optics
entries.hint: Ibn al-Haytham (Alhazen) came to Cairo under al-Hakim — the story goes, on a rash promise to regulate the Nile flood, which he could not keep. There he wrote the 'Book of Optics', which established by systematic experiment that vision works by light entering the eye, analysed reflection and refraction, and described the camera obscura. It is a founding document of the experimental method.
entries.note: Ibn al-Haytham, 'Kitab al-Manazir', trans. Sabra, 'The Optics of Ibn al-Haytham' (1989); the Latin 'Perspectiva' via Gerard of Cremona shaped Bacon, Witelo and Kepler. The Nile-dam anecdote is from Ibn Abi Usaybi'a (13th c.) and may be legend.

entries.label: Ibn Yunus and the Hakimi tables
entries.hint: The astronomer Ibn Yunus compiled the 'Hakimi Zij', the most careful set of astronomical tables of its age, based on decades of his own recorded observations of eclipses and conjunctions. Those dated observations were used a thousand years later by modern astronomers to measure the long-term slowing of the Earth's rotation.
entries.note: the 'al-Zij al-Kabir al-Hakimi'; King, 'A Survey of the Scientific Manuscripts of the Egyptian National Library' (1986); Newton's use of Ibn Yunus's eclipse records in the 20th-century tidal-friction studies.

entries.label: The House of Knowledge
entries.hint: Al-Hakim founded the Dar al-Ilm, a public library and teaching institution stocked from the palace collections and open to scholars of every discipline and, it seems, every faith. It housed the da'wa's teaching sessions but also grammar, medicine, astronomy and law, and it lasted, with interruptions, to the end of the dynasty.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi's 'Khitat', quoting al-Musabbihi; Halm, 'The Fatimids and their Traditions of Learning' (1997).

entries.label: The Cairo–Baghdad medical dispute
entries.hint: Ali ibn Ridwan, a self-taught Cairo physician who rose to head the profession in Egypt, carried on a famous long-distance quarrel with the Baghdad doctor Ibn Butlan over Galen, the value of book-learning versus apprenticeship, and whether a chick is warmer than a young bird. It is a vivid record of how medicine was argued in the 11th century.
entries.note: the polemical exchange edited by Schacht & Meyerhof, 'The Medico-Philosophical Controversy between Ibn Butlan of Baghdad and Ibn Ridwan of Cairo' (1937); Ibn Ridwan's autobiography survives.

entries.label: The Brethren of Purity enter the Ismaili canon
entries.hint: The 'Epistles of the Brethren of Purity', the Basran encyclopedia of the sciences, were taken up by the Fatimid and especially the later Tayyibi da'wa as an authoritative statement of the cosmos the imam presides over. A work of ambiguous origin became, in Ismaili hands, something close to scripture.
entries.note: 'Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa'; the debated Ismaili connection (Marquet; el-Bizri (ed.), 'The Ikhwan al-Safa and their Rasa'il', 2008). Cross-references the Abbasid folio's Ikhwan entry.
keywords: Epistles of the Brethren of Purity

entries.label: The chroniclers of Fatimid Egypt — mostly writing later
entries.hint: The great contemporary chronicle, al-Musabbihi's 13,000-page history of Egypt, survives only in a single volume and in quotation. The connected narrative of the dynasty comes from Ibn Muyassar (13th c.) and above all al-Maqrizi (d. 1442), whose 'Khitat' and 'Itti'az al-Hunafa' preserve lost Fatimid material at nearly five centuries' remove.
entries.note: the source situation is itself a research problem: Walker, 'Exploring an Islamic Empire: Fatimid History and its Sources' (2002), is the guide. The Geniza and the chancery documents (Rustow, 'The Lost Archive', 2020) partly compensate.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The India trade pulled to the Red Sea, the Geniza world, African gold, and the famine that broke the state

entries.label: The India trade moves to the Red Sea
entries.hint: Under the Fatimids the long-distance trade with India and the Far East shifted decisively from the Persian Gulf, which had carried it under the Abbasids, to the Red Sea route through Aden, up to the Egyptian ports and across to Alexandria. Cairo–Fustat became the great clearing-house between the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean.
entries.note: Goitein & Friedman, 'India Traders of the Middle Ages: Documents from the Cairo Geniza' (2008); the shift from the Gulf (see the Islamic Eastern Arabia folio).

entries.label: The Cairo Geniza — a documented commercial world
entries.hint: For religious reasons the Jews of Fustat did not throw away paper bearing the name of God — and so kept, in a synagogue storeroom, tens of thousands of ordinary documents: business letters, partnership contracts, bills of lading, marriage settlements, court records. It is the fullest picture of everyday medieval Mediterranean commerce and life that exists for any society.
entries.note: S. D. Goitein, 'A Mediterranean Society: The Jewish Communities of the Arab World as Portrayed in the Documents of the Cairo Geniza' (6 vols, 1967–93).

entries.label: West African gold
entries.hint: The gold that backed the Fatimid dinar came across the Sahara from the Sahel — from the goldfields of Bambuk and Bure through the caravan city of Sijilmasa. Control of that flow was a Fatimid war aim in the Maghreb, and its later diversion toward Almoravid Morocco was one cause of Fatimid Ifriqiya's decline.
entries.note: Messier, 'The Almoravids and the Meanings of Jihad' (2010), on the gold routes; Devisse in the 'General History of Africa' vol. 3; the numismatic evidence for gold sources.

entries.label: The Mustansirite famine
entries.hint: Seven successive low Niles, compounded by the army's blockade of the food supply and by plague, produced the worst famine in Egypt's recorded medieval history. The later sources — writing to dramatise the crisis and Badr al-Jamali's rescue — describe streets emptied, the palace stripped, and cannibalism. Whatever the exaggeration, the state did not function for a decade.
entries.note: al-Maqrizi's 'Ighathat al-Umma bi-Kashf al-Ghumma' (a treatise on Egyptian famines) and the 'Itti'az'; the topos and its uses (Brett, 'The Fatimid Empire', 2017, ch. 7).

entries.label: Fustat — a manufacturing and warehousing city
entries.hint: Below the royal enclosure of al-Qahira, Fustat was where the work was done: multi-storey apartment blocks, glass and pottery kilns, sugar refineries, paper mills, dye-houses, and the warehouses (funduqs and dar wakalas) where the India and Mediterranean goods were stored and taxed. Its rubbish mounds are still being excavated.
entries.note: the Fustat excavations (Scanlon; Kubiak, 'Al-Fustat: Its Foundation and Early Urban Development', 1987); the Geniza on housing and industry.

entries.label: The Italian merchants in Alexandria
entries.hint: Amalfitans first, then Venetians, Pisans and Genoese, kept warehouses and consuls in Alexandria and carried Egyptian alum, flax, sugar and spices to Europe against silver and timber. The Fatimids taxed the trade heavily and protected it; the relationship survived even the Crusades.
entries.note: the Italian and Geniza evidence for the Alexandria trade (Jacoby; Goitein); the treaties with Pisa (1154) and others survive in Latin and Arabic.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Experimental optics, the paper city, the war fleet, and Armenian fortification

entries.label: The experimental method in optics
entries.hint: Ibn al-Haytham's optics is not just a theory but a method: darkened rooms, apertures, tubes, screens and sighting instruments used to test claims against controlled observation, with the results reasoned through geometrically. It is the clearest medieval statement anywhere of science as deliberate experiment.
entries.note: Sabra's edition and commentary (1989); the apparatus described in the 'Manazir' books 1 and 7.

entries.label: A city built on paper
entries.hint: Fatimid Egypt ran on cheap paper: the chancery's decrees and petitions, the merchants' letters and account books, the shopping lists and school exercises later found in the Geniza. Egyptian paper mills supplied the eastern Mediterranean, and the survival of so much of it is why Fatimid daily life is so well known.
entries.note: Bloom, 'Paper Before Print' (2001); the physical range of the Geniza and chancery documents (Rustow, 'The Lost Archive', 2020).

entries.label: The Fatimid war fleet
entries.loc: the arsenals of Alexandria, Tinnis and Damietta
entries.hint: The Fatimids maintained a standing Mediterranean navy — a state arsenal, salaried crews, and squadrons that fought the Byzantines, raided the crusader coast and resupplied Ascalon four times a year until it fell. It was the last serious Muslim battle fleet in the Mediterranean before the Ottomans.
entries.note: Lev, 'The Fatimid Navy, Byzantium and the Mediterranean Sea 909–1036', Byzantion (1984); the Ascalon supply convoys (William of Tyre; Ibn al-Qalanisi).

entries.label: The stone walls and gates of Cairo
entries.hint: Badr al-Jamali's rebuilding of Cairo's enceinte in cut stone, with rounded and rectangular towers and vaulted gate-passages, brought Byzantine-frontier military architecture — carried by his Armenian engineers — into Egypt. The three surviving gates are the oldest stone monuments of medieval Cairo.
entries.note: Creswell, 'The Muslim Architecture of Egypt' vol. 1 (1952); the tradition that three Christian architects from Edessa built the gates (Maqrizi); comparison with Anatolian and Armenian fortification.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The da'wa across the Islamic world, the Armenian influx, the Sulayhid queen of Yemen, and the Franks

entries.label: The da'wa as a trans-regional network
entries.loc: from Sind to the Maghreb; secretly in Iraq and Iran
entries.hint: The Fatimid missionary organisation was the connective tissue of a movement that a single state could never contain: da'is in Yemen, Sind, Bahrain, Khurasan and the Maghreb, reporting toward Cairo, converting rulers and building cells inside the Abbasid world. The Persian poet Nasir Khusraw was recruited into it in Cairo and sent home to run the da'wa of Khurasan.
entries.note: Nasir Khusraw's own account in the 'Safarnama' and his poetry; Daftary, 'The Ismailis' (2007); Halm, 'The Fatimids and their Traditions of Learning' (1997).

entries.label: The Armenians come to Egypt
entries.hint: Badr al-Jamali, an Armenian, brought Armenian regiments, officials and their families to Egypt, and his son al-Afdal continued the settlement. Armenian viziers, an Armenian Coptic-rite church, Armenian craftsmen and the Armenian patriarchate all took root in Fatimid Cairo — a lasting community in a country that had none before.
entries.note: Dadoyan, 'The Fatimid Armenians: Cultural and Political Interaction in the Near East' (1997).

entries.label: The Sulayhid queen of Yemen
entries.hint: Arwa bint Ahmad, al-Sayyida al-Hurra, ruled Yemen for some seventy years as a Fatimid vassal, held the high da'wa rank of hujja, minted coins and had the Friday sermon read in her name. When the Musta'li da'wa split in 1132, the Tayyibi branch entrusted its leadership to her — a woman at the head of a religious hierarchy.
entries.note: the Yemeni Ismaili histories (Umara al-Yamani; the Tayyibi tradition); Cortese & Calderini, 'Women and the Fatimids in the World of Islam' (2006).

entries.label: Byzantium — the peace across the frontier
entries.hint: After the frontier fighting of the 960s–980s the Fatimids and Byzantines settled into a long working peace: trade treaties, an agreed protectorate over Aleppo, Byzantine grain sent to Egypt in famine years, and — after al-Hakim — Byzantine money and craftsmen rebuilding the Holy Sepulchre. Each empire even maintained a mosque or church for the other's merchants.
entries.note: Yahya of Antioch; the treaties in the Byzantine and Arabic sources (Canard; Felix, 'Byzanz und die islamische Welt im früheren 11. Jahrhundert', 1981).

entries.label: The Fatimids and the Franks
entries.hint: The Fatimids first approached the passing Crusaders as possible allies against the Seljuks, then fought them for sixty years over the coast, then — in their last decade — took a Frankish garrison into Cairo and paid Jerusalem an annual tribute against the Zangid threat. The relationship ran from alliance to war to dependence.
entries.note: the 1097–98 Fatimid–Crusader contacts (Köhler, 'Alliances and Treaties between Frankish and Muslim Rulers in the Middle East', 2013); William of Tyre and Ibn al-Athir on the 1160s.

entries.label: Fatimid style travels — Sicily and beyond
entries.hint: Fatimid ornament, ceramics, textiles and the muqarnas vault reached Norman Sicily directly — the painted wooden ceiling of the Cappella Palatina in Palermo is Fatimid work or close imitation of it — and Fatimid rock crystal and lustreware entered European treasuries and inspired local production. The counter-caliphate exported taste as well as gold.
entries.note: the Cappella Palatina ceiling (Grube & Johns, 'The Painted Ceilings of the Cappella Palatina', 2005); Contadini (1998); Jill Caskey on the Amalfitan connection.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: Three caliphates, the centre moved to Cairo, the Seljuk squeeze, the Crusades, and Saladin's restoration

entries.label: Three caliphates at once
entries.hint: The Fatimid proclamation of 909 broke the fiction of a single caliph; the Umayyad ruler of Córdoba answered with his own claim in 929. For the rest of the Middle Ages there were at least two, often three, men each insisting he alone led all Muslims. The Fatimids were the aggressive claimant — the others reacted to them.
entries.note: Halm, 'The Empire of the Mahdi' (1996); the Córdoban response (see the Al-Andalus 711–1031 folio). Cross-references the Abbasid folio.

entries.label: The centre of gravity moves to Cairo
entries.hint: The founding of Cairo created the city that would be the largest and richest in the Islamic world for the next six centuries — the seat of the Fatimid, then Ayyubid, then Mamluk states, the hinge of the India trade, and eventually the refuge of the Abbasid caliphate itself. The Fatimids built the capital of the later medieval Middle East.
entries.note: Raymond, 'Cairo' (2000); the long-run demographic and economic primacy of Fatimid-founded Cairo.

entries.label: The Seljuk squeeze
entries.hint: The arrival of the Sunni Seljuks in Syria caught the Fatimids between a resurgent Abbasid orthodoxy to the north-east and their own internal collapse. They lost Damascus, Jerusalem and the interior of Palestine, and recovered only the coast and a briefly-held Jerusalem — the strategic position from which they faced the Crusade.
entries.note: Ibn al-Qalanisi; the Seljuk advance (see the Abbasid folio); Brett (2017).

entries.label: The Crusades and the Fatimid misjudgement
entries.hint: Cairo read the First Crusade as another band of Frankish mercenaries who might be turned against the Seljuks, and opened negotiations. By the time the mistake was clear the Crusaders held Jerusalem, and the Fatimids spent their last productive decades in a losing coastal war against a state they had helped to establish.
entries.note: Köhler (2013); Hillenbrand, 'The Crusades: Islamic Perspectives' (1999); the 1098 embassy in the 'Gesta Francorum'.

entries.label: Egypt returns to Sunni Islam
entries.hint: Saladin's suppression of the caliphate in 1171 met almost no resistance because the Ismaili state had never made Egypt Ismaili. Within a generation the Ayyubids had covered Cairo in Sunni madrasas, the da'wa had gone underground or emigrated to Yemen and India, and the Fatimid palaces had been given away as barracks and stables.
entries.note: Lyons & Jackson, 'Saladin' (1982); the Ayyubid 'Sunnisation' of Egypt (Leiser, 'The Restoration of Sunnism in Egypt', 1976).

entries.label: The afterlives of the Fatimid da'wa
entries.hint: The state ended in 1171 but the movement did not: the Nizari line produced the Aga Khans; the Tayyibi line, carried from Yemen to Gujarat, produced the Bohra communities; and the Druze survived in Syria and Lebanon. Three living communities trace their authority through the Fatimid imams of Cairo.
entries.note: Daftary, 'The Ismailis: Their History and Doctrines' (2nd ed. 2007), parts 3–4; the modern communities.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: A queen who led a religious hierarchy, the Geniza's ordinary people, the ethnic regiments, and al-Hakim

entries.label: Women of power — Sitt al-Mulk and Queen Arwa
entries.hint: Al-Hakim's sister Sitt al-Mulk ran the Egyptian state as regent after his disappearance; the Sulayhid queen Arwa ruled Yemen for seventy years and held the da'wa rank of hujja, the highest a person other than the imam could reach. Fatimid ideology, which located authority in a bloodline rather than in maleness, made room for both.
entries.note: Cortese & Calderini, 'Women and the Fatimids in the World of Islam' (2006); the coins struck in Arwa's name.

entries.label: The Geniza people
entries.hint: The Geniza lets us follow individuals: the India trader Abraham Ben Yiju, who married and freed an Indian slave woman and raised a family on the Malabar coast; the widow petitioning the court over her dowry; the schoolboy's copybook; the letter from a man stranded without funds in a foreign port. It is medieval life at eye level, in the words of the people living it.
entries.note: Goitein, 'A Mediterranean Society' vol. 3 (the family) and vol. 5 (the individual); Goitein & Friedman, 'India Traders' (2008); Ghosh, 'In an Antique Land' (1992), a literary reconstruction of Ben Yiju.

entries.label: The ethnic regiments and the army that tore the state apart
entries.hint: The Fatimid army was a mosaic of recruited and enslaved groups kept deliberately separate — Kutama Berbers, then Turkish and Daylami cavalry, then large regiments of Black African infantry (the 'Abid al-Shira), then Armenians. Under a weak caliph in a famine they fought each other rather than the enemy, and the civil war of 1062–73 nearly ended the dynasty.
entries.note: Lev, 'Army, Regime, and Society in Fatimid Egypt', IJMES (1987); Beshir, 'Fatimid Military Organization', Der Islam (1978).

entries.label: Slavery in the Fatimid world
entries.loc: Cairo; the Nile route; the Red Sea
entries.hint: Enslaved people reached Egypt down the Nile from Nubia and across the Red Sea from the Horn and East Africa, and by the Mediterranean from Europe: military slaves in the Black regiments, eunuch officials at the centre of the palace, and the domestic slaves — many women — whose lives fill the Geniza's marriage contracts, manumission deeds and court cases.
entries.note: the Geniza on domestic slavery (Goitein vol. 1); the military slavery (Lev 1987); the Nubian 'baqt' treaty tradition governing the Nile slave supply.

entries.label: The palace eunuchs
entries.hint: Eunuchs — enslaved as boys, castrated outside the empire, and raised in the palace — held some of the highest offices of the Fatimid state: the tutors of caliphs, the keepers of the treasuries and the harem, commanders of armies, and occasionally the effective rulers. They were a recognised third category at the centre of power.
entries.note: the Fatimid eunuch officials in the sources (Ibn al-Tuwayr; al-Maqrizi); Ayalon, 'Eunuchs, Caliphs and Sultans' (1999); Marmon, 'Eunuchs and Sacred Boundaries in Islamic Society' (1995).

entries.label: Al-Hakim — the caliph as an enigma
entries.hint: No medieval Muslim ruler is harder to read than al-Hakim: an ascetic who gave away his wealth and rode a donkey; a persecutor who then made restitution; a lawgiver who banned women from the streets and mulukhiyya from the table; a man whose followers declared him God and who vanished, at 36, into the hills. The sources cannot agree whether he was mad, calculating, or a saint.
entries.note: Walker, 'Caliph of Cairo: al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, 996–1021' (2009), sifts the contradictory material; the Druze reading, the Sunni condemnation and the Fatimid embarrassment are all present in the tradition.
